unit.title: How a Grand Prix weekend works
unit.summary: What F1 is, who competes, how a weekend flows and how points work.

lessons.title: What Formula 1 actually is
lessons.objective: Explain F1 as a world championship of teams and drivers across roughly 23 races.

payload.prompt: Roughly how many races make up a modern F1 season?

explanation.correct: About 23 Grands Prix, spread from March to December. The exact calendar shifts from year to year, so think 'a couple of dozen'.
explanation.incorrect: A modern season has about 23 Grands Prix, one at each venue from March to December. It was 16 to 17 in the 1990s, so the sport has grown a lot.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is a long season, about twenty-three races.

payload.prompt: What is a constructor in F1?

options.text: A team that builds its own car and scores in the championship
options.explanation: Constructors like Ferrari and McLaren build their own cars; they compete for both titles.

options.text: Only the engine supplier
options.explanation: An engine supplier builds power units, often for other teams. A constructor is the team that builds the car and scores constructors' points.

options.text: The driver's team manager
options.explanation: The team principal runs the team, but that is not the same as a constructor.

options.text: The company that supplies the tyres
options.explanation: Tyres come from one official supplier, Pirelli. That is a different job from building the car.

explanation.correct: A constructor is a team that competes for the constructors' championship by building its own car.
explanation.incorrect: A constructor is a team that builds its own car. It is different from a supplier or manager.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari is a constructor with its own engines and team.

payload.prompt: Can the drivers' champion drive for a team that misses the constructors' title?

scene.alt: Text only: one driver wins the individual title while his team finishes behind a rival in the team standings.

choices.label: No, the same team wins both

explanation.correct: The two titles are counted separately. The drivers' title is one person's points; the constructors' title adds both of a team's drivers, so a star with a weaker teammate can win one and not the other.
explanation.incorrect: They are two separate tables. One driver's total decides the drivers' title; both drivers' points added together decide the constructors' title, so different winners are possible.
explanation.sayThisLine: He won the drivers' title, but the team lost the constructors' fight.

payload.prompt: Match each term to what it is.

pairs.definition: One race round of the world championship at one circuit.
A team that builds its own car and scores points for the constructors' title.
The season-long title fight decided by accumulated points.

distractorDefinitions: The final race of the season
A penalty for breaking the rules

explanation.summary: A Grand Prix is one race; a constructor is a team; the championship is the whole season.
explanation.sayThisLine: We are fighting for the championship all season.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: Who builds the fastest car matters more than who drives it.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The car is a huge part of the fight
options.explanation: The machine is a major factor in results.

options.text: The driver does not matter
options.explanation: She is not dismissing drivers. Her point is that the car is a big part of the result; the driver still matters.

options.text: The constructors' title is worth more than the drivers' one
options.explanation: She is talking about how much the car matters to results, not about which trophy is bigger.

payload.translation: She thinks the quality of the car is the main variable in the championship fight.

followUps.line: Do you think the teammate battle proves that, or disproves it?
followUps.why: Tests if you know the teammate is the fairest comparison.

followUps.line: Does one great driver in a mediocre car ever win a title?
followUps.why: Invites historical or strategic thinking without pretending.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Avoid saying "it's just the driver." Car and driver both matter, and the teammate battle is how we tell.

lessons.title: Who is on the grid in 2026
lessons.objective: Name the 11 teams and explain works versus customer teams.

payload.prompt: Match each team to its engine supplier in 2026.

pairs.definition: Works team with its own engines; also supplies Haas and Cadillac.
Works team and engine supplier to McLaren, Williams and Alpine.
Works-style partnership with Ford engines; also runs Racing Bulls.

explanation.summary: Ferrari, Mercedes and Red Bull (with Ford) all build their own power units. Audi is brand new to the grid as an engine maker, and Honda is back, partnered with Aston Martin.
explanation.sayThisLine: Mercedes supplies engines to three teams.

payload.prompt: Match each team to its category.

pairs.definition: Builds its own engine and usually its own car.
Buys engines from a supplier and competes independently.
New works team power unit joining in 2026.

explanation.summary: Works teams like Ferrari own their engines; customer teams like Williams buy theirs.
explanation.sayThisLine: McLaren is a customer team on Mercedes power.

payload.prompt: Which of these is a works team in 2026?

options.text: Ferrari
options.explanation: Ferrari builds its own engines and cars; it is a full works team.

options.text: Williams
options.explanation: Williams buys Mercedes engines and is a customer team.

options.text: McLaren
options.explanation: McLaren buys Mercedes engines and is a customer team.

options.text: Alpine
options.explanation: Alpine switched to Mercedes power for 2026 and is now a customer team.

explanation.correct: Ferrari is a works team: it builds its own power unit and its own car. Mercedes, Audi, Red Bull-Ford and Honda (with Aston Martin) are the other works power units in 2026.
explanation.incorrect: In 2026 the works-style teams are Ferrari, Mercedes, Audi, Red Bull (with Ford) and Aston Martin (with Honda). Williams, McLaren, Alpine, Haas, Racing Bulls and Cadillac use someone else's power unit.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari is a works team with its own engines.

payload.prompt: How many teams are on the 2026 grid?

options.explanation: That was the count for years up to 2025. Cadillac's arrival made it one more.
Cadillac joined in 2026, bringing the grid to 11 teams with 22 drivers.
Too few; the grid has just grown, not shrunk.
There are 11 teams on the 2026 grid.

explanation.correct: Cadillac is the 11th team, joining in 2026 on Ferrari power. That means 22 drivers total.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 grid has 11 teams: Ferrari, McLaren, Mercedes, Red Bull, Racing Bulls, Haas, Williams, Alpine, Aston Martin, Audi and Cadillac.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eleven teams on the 2026 grid, with Cadillac as the new one.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence.
payload.template: A {{team-type}} team buys {{what}} from a supplier, while a {{other-type}} team builds its own.

explanation.correct: A customer team buys engines; a works team builds its own.
explanation.incorrect: Customer teams buy engines from suppliers. Works teams design and build their own power units.
explanation.sayThisLine: McLaren is a customer team on Mercedes power.

lessons.title: Friday to Sunday
lessons.objective: Put the parts of a race weekend in order and say what each is for.

payload.prompt: Put a race weekend in order.

items.why: Teams learn the track and test set-ups and tyres; nobody wins anything here.

items.text: Parc ferme rules: set-ups are locked
items.why: Once qualifying starts, teams can barely change the car; it stays locked.
Fastest single laps set the grid; the top ten go through each round.
Drivers warm up tyres and brakes before lining up on the grid.
Five red lights go out and the field launches for roughly 305 km.
The race ends; the first driver to finish wins.

explanation.correct: Friday practice, then qualifying (with parc ferme), formation lap, lights out, and the chequered flag.
explanation.incorrect: Order: practice → parc ferme → qualifying → formation lap → start → chequered flag.
explanation.sayThisLine: The weekend flows from practice on Friday through Sunday's race.

payload.prompt: What is the main purpose of Friday free practice?

options.text: Teams test set-ups and tyres; nobody scores points
options.explanation: Practice is purely for learning and preparation; it does not affect the race result.

options.text: It is a qualifying session to set the grid
options.explanation: Qualifying on Saturday sets the grid, not practice.

options.text: Drivers race on Friday to warm up
options.explanation: Practice is controlled running, not a race.

options.text: The team decides who will drive on Sunday
options.explanation: The drivers are already selected; practice just tunes the car.

explanation.correct: Friday practice is for learning the circuit, testing components and finding set-up clues. No points are at stake.
explanation.incorrect: Practice sessions are for preparation only. Qualifying and the race are the scored events.
explanation.sayThisLine: Friday is where they learn the track and find the car's balance.

payload.prompt: Once qualifying starts, what does parc ferme mean?

options.text: The car set-up is locked; teams can barely change it
options.explanation: Parc ferme means the cars are 'locked' and protected from major changes between qualifying and the race.

options.text: All cars must pit for new tyres
options.explanation: Parc ferme is about the lock on changes, not a pit mandate.

options.text: The race is delayed for safety
options.explanation: That would be a red flag or VSC, not parc ferme.

options.text: Drivers must stay in the paddock
options.explanation: Parc ferme is about the car, not the driver's location.

explanation.correct: Parc ferme means the cars are locked from major changes once qualifying starts.
explanation.incorrect: Parc ferme locks the car set-up once qualifying begins, preventing big changes before the race.
explanation.sayThisLine: Once parc ferme is on, no more big changes.

payload.prompt: What does the formation lap do?

options.text: Lets drivers warm up tyres and brakes before the start
options.explanation: The formation lap is a warm-up lap where drivers heat their rubber and brakes.

options.text: It is when the grid is set for the race
options.explanation: The grid is set by qualifying; the formation lap is the warm-up.

options.text: It decides how many pit stops each team must make
options.explanation: Strategy and tyre rules decide stops, not the formation lap.

options.text: The first official lap of the race
options.explanation: The formation lap is separate; the race starts with lights out after.

explanation.correct: The formation lap is where drivers heat their tyres and brakes and line up on the grid.
explanation.incorrect: The formation lap warms up the car for the start. Then lights out begins the race.
explanation.sayThisLine: The formation lap is where drivers warm up the tyres and brakes.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about the weekend order.
payload.template: {{first}} comes before {{second}}, and parc ferme rules start when {{third}} begins.

explanation.correct: Practice is first (Friday); qualifying is second (Saturday); parc ferme locks the car once qualifying starts.
explanation.incorrect: The order is practice on Friday, then qualifying on Saturday, when parc ferme rules kick in.
explanation.sayThisLine: Practice first, then qualifying, and parc ferme locks it down.

lessons.title: Q1, Q2, Q3: the knockout
lessons.objective: Explain how qualifying sets the grid and why pole matters.

payload.prompt: He ends Q1 in 16th place. Does he go through to Q2?

scene.alt: Text only: a 20-car field, and one driver has just been bumped down to 16th on the Q1 timing screen.

explanation.correct: Q1 cuts the slowest five cars, so 16th to 20th are out and keep those grid spots. The fastest 15 go on to Q2, where five more drop out.
explanation.incorrect: Only the fastest 15 survive Q1. Anyone from 16th down is eliminated and starts the race in that slot.
explanation.sayThisLine: Q1 knocked out the slowest five, so he will start 16th.

payload.prompt: How much does it matter to start first on the grid (pole position)?

options.text: It matters a lot; how much depends on the track
options.explanation: At tight circuits like Monaco or Singapore, pole is huge. At Monza with long straights, it matters less.

options.text: It does not matter; the race is what counts
options.explanation: True that the race decides everything, but track position is valuable everywhere.

options.text: It matters more than the car's speed
options.explanation: Pole helps, but car speed and strategy are the main factors.

options.text: Pole guarantees a win
options.explanation: Pole is an advantage, not a guarantee; races are decided by speed, strategy and luck.

explanation.correct: Pole is most valuable at tight, hard-to-pass tracks like Monaco. At high-speed circuits it is less critical.
explanation.incorrect: Pole gives track position, which is worth more at some tracks than others.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pole at Monaco is basically the race. At Monza it is less.

payload.prompt: He is first in Q3 after his first run. Should he pit for new tyres and run again?

scene.alt: Text only: he leads qualifying with one lap left in the final session.

choices.label: Run again on fresh tyres for pole
Sit in the garage and hope

explanation.correct: Only a driver's best lap counts, so a second run cannot cost him the time he already has. It can only improve it, and rivals may well go quicker, so sitting still is the riskier move.
explanation.incorrect: His first lap stays on the board even if a second run goes wrong, so running again is close to free. Waiting lets rivals with a fresh run leapfrog him.
explanation.sayThisLine: He went out again and nailed pole.

payload.prompt: As cars lay rubber, the track grows grippier. When are the fastest laps usually set?

scene.alt: Text only: a qualifying session in which the circuit surface is getting quicker with every lap driven on it.

explanation.correct: Track evolution means grip builds as rubber goes down, so the last runs are usually the quickest. That is why teams save their best tyres for the end of a session.
explanation.incorrect: The surface improves as more cars drive on it, so times tumble late in a session. Early laps are slower, which is why the final runs matter most.
explanation.sayThisLine: The track is evolving, so everyone will go quicker at the end.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about qualifying.
payload.template: Q1 eliminates the slowest {{count1}} cars, Q2 does the same to the next {{count2}}, and Q3 is for the {{count3}} fastest to fight for pole.

explanation.correct: Q1: top 15 advance (5 eliminated). Q2: top 10 advance (5 more out). Q3: the final 10 race for pole.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying is a knockout: Q1 (20→15), Q2 (15→10), Q3 (10 fight for pole).
explanation.sayThisLine: He made Q3, so he is in the top ten for pole day.

lessons.title: Lights out to chequered flag
lessons.objective: Walk through a race from formation lap to the flag.

payload.prompt: Put the key moments of a race start in order.

items.text: Formation lap: drivers warm up tyres and line up
items.why: The warm-up lap heats the rubber and brakes, and the grid lines up.

items.text: Lights go out; the start is live
items.why: Five red lights extinguish and the field launches.
The first lap is the wildest as drivers jostle for position.

items.text: The race settles into its rhythm
items.why: After turn one, the order stabilizes until the pit window opens.
The first driver to cross scores the win and 25 points.

explanation.correct: Formation lap → lights out → turn one chaos → settled race → chequered flag.
explanation.incorrect: The race flow: formation lap and warm-up, lights out, first-lap chaos, steady running, then the flag.
explanation.sayThisLine: The start decided everything; he gained three places in turn one.

payload.prompt: How far is a typical Grand Prix race?

explanation.correct: A Grand Prix is roughly 305 km (Monaco is shorter at about 260 km). It is also capped at two hours of racing time.
explanation.incorrect: A Grand Prix is run over the smallest whole number of laps that adds up to more than 305 km, so most are about 305 to 310 km. Monaco is the exception at about 260 km.
explanation.sayThisLine: The race is about 305 kilometres.

payload.prompt: What is the chequered flag?

options.text: The flag that ends the race for each driver as they cross the line
options.explanation: The chequered flag signals the finish; the race is over for that driver.

options.text: A flag that warns of danger
options.explanation: Yellow and red flags warn; the chequered flag ends the race.

options.text: Shown only to the winner
options.explanation: Every driver gets a chequered flag as they finish; it ends their race.

options.text: A penalty for bad driving
options.explanation: The chequered flag ends the race, not a penalty.

explanation.correct: The chequered flag ends each driver's race as they cross the line. The first to see it wins.
explanation.incorrect: The chequered flag finishes the race. Every driver gets it when they cross; the leader gets it first and wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: He took the chequered flag in first place.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about how a race ends.
payload.template: The race ends after the set number of laps, or once {{limit}} of racing time have passed, whichever comes first.

explanation.correct: Two hours of racing time is the cap. Most races finish their laps well inside it; slow running behind a safety car is what can push a race up against the limit.
explanation.incorrect: The time cap is two hours. Most races finish all their laps in about an hour and a half, but safety cars eat clock without adding laps.
explanation.sayThisLine: They ran out of time before they ran out of laps.

payload.prompt: At lights out, 20 cars rush one corner. Is contact more likely there than mid-race?

scene.alt: Text only: a full grid accelerating side by side towards the first corner of a race.

choices.label: Yes, turn one is the risky bit
No, it is the same all race

explanation.correct: At the start the whole field is bunched, cars are side by side, and everyone is fighting for the same piece of road. That is why first-lap incidents are common and why fans watch turn one.
explanation.incorrect: Turn one is riskier than most of the race: the cars are packed together and tyres are still coming up to temperature. Later the field spreads out and there is more room.
explanation.sayThisLine: Turn one is always a lottery, so I am watching that bit closely.

lessons.title: Points, podiums and the two titles
lessons.objective: Score a race and explain how both championships work.

payload.prompt: How many points does a Grand Prix win score?

explanation.correct: A win is 25 points. Second place gets 18, third gets 15. The scale runs 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 for the top ten.
explanation.incorrect: The winner scores 25 points in 2026. There is no bonus for fastest lap since 2025.
explanation.sayThisLine: A win is 25 points, so a DNF really hurts.

payload.prompt: What is the podium?

options.text: The top three finishers who spray champagne
options.explanation: The podium is where P1, P2 and P3 climb and celebrate.

options.text: The winner's celebration area
options.explanation: The podium includes all top three; it is not just the winner.

options.text: The pit lane area
options.explanation: The podium is the celebration platform, not the pit lane.

options.text: A penalty for poor performance
options.explanation: The podium is a honour, not a penalty.

explanation.correct: The podium is the ceremony for the top three drivers; they climb the platform and spray champagne.
explanation.incorrect: The podium celebrates P1, P2 and P3. It is held after the race and is one of F1's defining moments.
explanation.sayThisLine: He made the podium in third place!

payload.prompt: One driver wins (25 points) and his teammate is tenth (1 point). What does the team score?

scene.alt: Text only: a team's two cars finish first and tenth in the same race.

explanation.correct: Both cars score for the constructors' table, so 25 plus 1 makes 26. That is why a strong second driver matters so much to the team title.
explanation.incorrect: The constructors' title adds up both drivers' points, so the tenth-place car still counts. The team scores 26, not just the winner's 25.
explanation.sayThisLine: Both cars score for the team, so the second driver matters too.

payload.prompt: What happened to the fastest-lap bonus point from 2025?

options.text: It was removed; there is no bonus point for fastest lap anymore
options.explanation: The fastest-lap bonus point is gone since 2025; it is now bragging rights only.

options.text: It is now worth 3 points
options.explanation: It was worth 1 point when it existed; now it is worth nothing.

options.text: Only the top three can score it
options.explanation: The fastest lap was never restricted to podium finishers; any driver could set it.

options.text: It is now the most valuable point
options.explanation: Fastest lap is bragging rights only now; winning the race (25 points) is what matters.

explanation.correct: For 2025 onwards, there is no bonus point for fastest lap. It is a stat but not a championship point.
explanation.incorrect: The fastest-lap point was removed for 2025. Now the top ten score 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1; that's it.
explanation.sayThisLine: No fastest-lap point since 2025; it's just pride now.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about scoring.
payload.template: A Grand Prix win is {{points}} points, second is {{second}}, and third is {{third}}.

explanation.correct: Win: 25. Second: 18. Third: 15. Fourth to tenth: 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2, 1. Fastest lap is bragging rights only.
explanation.incorrect: The points scale is 25-18-15-12-10-8-6-4-2-1 for positions 1-10. Fastest lap scores zero points since 2025.
explanation.sayThisLine: A win is 25 points, so a DNF really hurts.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about championships.
payload.template: The {{individual}} championship is for the top driver; the {{team}} championship is both drivers' points added.

explanation.correct: Drivers' title: individual. Constructors' title: team total.
explanation.incorrect: Two championships run in parallel: drivers' (one person) and constructors' (the team's combined score).
explanation.sayThisLine: The team is pushing hard for the constructors' championship.

lessons.title: Sprint weekends
lessons.objective: Explain how a sprint weekend differs and what a sprint is worth.

payload.prompt: Put a sprint weekend schedule in order.

items.why: One FP1 session to learn the track.

items.text: Sprint qualifying (SQ1, SQ2, SQ3) on Friday
items.why: A knockout session to set the sprint grid (like regular qualifying but shorter).
A short race (about 100 km) that scores points for the top eight.
Sets the grid for Sunday's main race.
The main race that decides the weekend.

explanation.correct: Friday: FP1 and sprint qualifying. Saturday: sprint race, then GP qualifying. Sunday: the Grand Prix.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint weekends compress the schedule: sprint qualifying and race on Saturday, then Sunday's main race.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sprint weekends are busy; he qualified for the race on Friday.

payload.prompt: How many points does winning the sprint award?

scene.alt: Text only: he won the short race on Saturday.

explanation.correct: A sprint awards 8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1 to the top eight finishers. A win is worth 8, not the 25 of a Grand Prix.
explanation.incorrect: The sprint is worth less than a Grand Prix. Winning scores 8 points, not the full 25.
explanation.sayThisLine: The sprint is worth eight to the winner.

payload.prompt: The sprint winner starts from pole for the Grand Prix. True or false?

scene.alt: Text only: he won the Saturday sprint and now it is Sunday's main race.

choices.label: False; GP qualifying sets the grid

explanation.correct: The sprint winner does not get automatic pole for the GP. Saturday's GP qualifying sets Sunday's grid.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint and Grand Prix are separate events. GP qualifying on Saturday sets Sunday's grid, not the sprint result.
explanation.sayThisLine: He won the sprint but finished third in qualifying.

payload.prompt: About how long is a sprint race?

explanation.correct: A sprint is about 100 km, roughly a third of a Grand Prix's 305 km. It is short enough to fit on a Saturday and is flat out from the start.
explanation.incorrect: A sprint is only about 100 km, roughly a third of the Sunday race. There is no mandatory pit stop, so it is a short, sharp dash.
explanation.sayThisLine: The sprint is about a hundred kilometres, a third of the Sunday race.

payload.prompt: What gets squeezed for teams on a sprint weekend?

options.text: Practice: only one session before the serious running starts
options.explanation: Sprint weekends have a single practice session, so teams must find a good set-up quickly.

options.text: Qualifying: there is none on a sprint weekend
options.explanation: There is still qualifying for the Grand Prix, plus a separate sprint qualifying session.

options.text: The Grand Prix itself: it is cut to 100 km
options.explanation: The Sunday Grand Prix keeps its full distance of about 305 km. The sprint is the extra short race.

options.text: Championship points: none are given for the sprint
options.explanation: The sprint does score points, 8 down to 1 for the top eight.

explanation.correct: With one practice session before sprint qualifying begins, teams have much less time to learn the car and the tyres. It rewards teams that get the set-up right early.
explanation.incorrect: The squeeze is on practice: a sprint weekend has just one session. Qualifying, the sprint points and the full Sunday Grand Prix are all still there.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is a sprint weekend, so they only get one practice session.

lessons.title: Your first Sunday text
lessons.objective: Understand a fan's plain race-day message and reply naturally.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: He got a penalty so he lost three places on the grid. And it's not even his fault.

payload.question: What happened to him?

options.text: He was penalised for something during the race
options.explanation: She said he lost grid places, so this is before the race.

options.text: He took a new engine part, so the stewards dropped him three spots
options.explanation: Grid penalties for using more power unit parts than the season allows are common, and they cost places on the grid. The team chose the swap, so a fan can say it is 'not his fault'.

options.text: He crashed in qualifying and lost pole
options.explanation: A crash does not cost grid places by itself. Losing places on the grid is a penalty, handed out before the race.

options.text: He was disqualified from qualifying
options.explanation: Losing three places is a grid penalty, not a disqualification. He still races, from further back.

payload.translation: He got a grid penalty that dropped him places on the starting order, and she thinks he did not deserve it.

followUps.line: What was the penalty for—a technical thing like an engine part, or something he did?
followUps.why: Shows you understand penalties can be for different reasons.

followUps.line: Is he still in a good spot on the grid, or did he drop too far?
followUps.why: Respects her knowledge of the grid positions.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Do not pretend to know what the penalty was. Ask a real question.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: He was DNF in qualifying, so he couldn't even make the grid.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: He crashed or broke down during qualifying and didn't set a time
options.explanation: A DNF in qualifying means he didn't finish the session and has no qualifying time.

options.text: He retired from the race
options.explanation: She said 'in qualifying', not the race.

options.text: He was very slow and at the bottom of the grid
options.explanation: A slow time is not a DNF; a DNF is not finishing the session.

options.text: He was told he is banned from the next race
options.explanation: Nothing here suggests a ban. She means his qualifying went wrong, and it puts his Sunday start in doubt.

payload.translation: He crashed or had a mechanical failure during qualifying and never set a lap time, so his place on Sunday's grid is in doubt. Strictly, 'DNF' is a race word, so fans are being casual.

followUps.line: Is it a crash, or did the car break?
followUps.why: Shows you are curious about the reason.

followUps.line: Will the stewards let him start from the back anyway?
followUps.why: Shows you know a missed time is not always the end of the weekend.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A DNF in qualifying is rare and harsh. Ask what went wrong rather than guessing.

payload.prompt: Sarah says: 'He's on pole for tomorrow.' What does that mean?

options.text: He starts first on the grid
options.explanation: Pole position means he qualified fastest and gets the prime starting spot.

options.text: He will definitely win the race
options.explanation: Pole is an advantage, not a guarantee of victory.

options.text: He is in trouble with the stewards
options.explanation: A pole is not a penalty; it is the best grid spot.

options.text: He qualified on used tyres
options.explanation: The tyres he used in qualifying do not define pole; speed does.

explanation.correct: Pole position is first on the grid; he set the fastest lap in qualifying.
explanation.incorrect: When a fan says someone is 'on pole', they mean he or she qualified first and starts at the front.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's on pole, so he's got track position.

payload.prompt: Complete what Sarah might say about the podium.
payload.template: The {{first}} finisher gets the podium, along with {{second}} and {{third}}. It is an honour to be there.

explanation.correct: The podium is for the top three finishers: first place (the winner), second place and third place.
explanation.incorrect: Podium means the top three drivers spray champagne and celebrate on the platform.
explanation.sayThisLine: He made the podium in third; that is a great result.
